chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Safwan from Ibn Mukhan from al-Mu'alla ibn Khunays said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): What is sufficient in Mut'ah (temporary marriage) from the witnesses? He said: 'One man and two women who witness it.' I said: What if you see that they do not find anyone? He said: 'They will not lack [witnesses].' I said: What if you see that they fear that someone will know about it? Is it sufficient for them one man? He said: 'Yes.'
He said: I said: May I be your ransom, were the Muslims during the time of the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) to marry without a clear proof? He said: 'No.'

For indeed this report does not contain prohibition of Mut'ah except with a clear proof, and it is merely informing about what was during the time of the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) that they did not marry except with a clear proof, and that is the more excellent.

And it is not that if that was not occurring in that era, it indicates that it is forbidden, just as we know that here there are many things from the permissible acts and others that were not used in that time, and that was not an indication of its prohibition.
And so that the woman does not believe that that is not permissible if she is not from the people of knowledge, and that which reveals what we mentioned is what he narrated:
ai.seo_question: What are the witness requirements for temporary marriage (Mut'ah) in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) clarifies that while one man and two women are the standard witnesses for Mut'ah, necessity or fear of exposure permits even a single witness. He elucidates that the requirement of witnesses is not a prohibition of validity without them, but rather reflects the superior practice (istihbab) of the Prophet's companions, distinguishing between what was customary then and what is obligatory now. This distinction highlights the Shia principle that absence of a specific practice in the early era does not imply its prohibition, but rather indicates flexibility in application.
